name: Bianca Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We’re independent of AI companies, employers, unions, political parties and government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does an ordinary workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43 and a new supervisor of seven people who book appliance repair visits for a large manufacturer. I check the unfilled appointment board, move technicians between jobs and answer calls when someone has already waited all day. I like finally getting a repair visit into a family’s week. I’m still learning to manage the team and sometimes miss which technician has the right part, which means another angry call.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who is at home, and what could you manage if the company cut your hours?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband, Leon, drives delivery vans; our children are ten and thirteen, and the mortgage takes a large slice of our wages. My pay is low for a supervisor, we have less than a month saved and there are hardly any other big service offices around here. I have a bachelor’s degree, but I only moved into management this year and I’m still behind the senior supervisors. I like the paper appointment board; I’ve never used an AI tool and am slow to trust a new system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team to keep the repair board accurate and not promise callers that a new tool will fix missed visits. We still need to know which van has the right part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my job in this picture, but that does not settle the mortgage or Leon’s changing route hours. We have almost nothing to fall back on if his van breaks down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d keep the morning board check and ask the parts clerk to confirm every unusual repair before I move a van. In the first year I’d cut the children’s extra streaming package and hold the 18 a month against the next car repair bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the household even though the office carries on. A quiet AI story would not make my husband’s delivery van dependable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the children mind losing the streaming package?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They would complain for a week, then borrow films from the library. I’d rather explain that than have a van repair put the mortgage at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the paper board slow the team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sometimes it does, and I know that. I trust it because I can see every van move; I have not learned to trust the computer board yet.

say: I’d keep the **repair board** accurate for every scheduled visit.
Callers need a **real van and part**, and I would not mark a missed visit solved until both are confirmed.
think: Leon’s **variable routes** and our mortgage keep home money tight.
A **van repair** could take our remaining cash before the mortgage is due.
do: Check the **board each morning** and confirm unusual parts with the clerk.
Cancel the **extra streaming package** to protect money for a van repair.
feel: I feel **anxious** about our fragile household budget.
S0.quote: A quiet AI story would not make my husband’s delivery van dependable.
fieldNote: She trusts the **visible board** but admits it can be slow.
The job remains while **route hours and repairs** threaten the mortgage.
She cuts a specific **18 monthly cost** for a likely van bill.

steps.text: Keep morning appointment board checks and confirm unusual parts with the clerk
Cancel the children’s extra streaming package to free 18 monthly for van repairs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the new booking system should be tested against real missed visits before the company cuts the phone desk. I’d tell customers there must still be a person to call when a repair van is late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The software could book appointments and answer the standard questions that fill my day. As the newest and least skilled supervisor, I think I would be the first manager moved out if the desk shrank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d ask the senior supervisor to show me a week of computer bookings beside my paper board. In the first year I’d take the company’s paid training on that booking screen only if the test catches the wrong-part visits, and I’d ask our manager for a written list of roles still needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m alarmed because I can see my own post going, not just a clerk’s. I’m willing to watch a proper test, but I cannot afford an unpaid course or a gap in wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a proper test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Put twenty real repair jobs through both boards and check the address, part and available van. If the screen misses a broken freezer visit, the caller pays for our lesson.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the tool tomorrow if the senior supervisor liked it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would watch first and compare the bookings myself. I have never used AI, and one person’s enthusiasm is not enough to risk a customer’s day.

say: I’d demand a **missed-visit test** before cutting the desk.
Customers still need a **human phone contact** for late vans.
think: My junior standing makes me fear being the **first manager cut**.
With **thin savings**, I cannot wait long for another role.
do: Compare **twenty repair jobs** on the screen and paper board.
Take **paid booking training** only if the tool catches wrong-part visits.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about losing my post and wages.
S1.quote: If the screen misses a broken freezer visit, the caller pays for our lesson.
fieldNote: She needs **twenty actual jobs** before trusting the screen.
She recognizes that she is the **newest manager** on an exposed desk.
Her first tool training is **paid and conditional** on finding wrong-part visits.

steps.text: Compare twenty real repair bookings on the computer screen and paper board
Complete paid booking-screen training only if the test catches wrong-part visits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the office to give families a real number to call after an automated booking goes wrong. I’d ask management what happens to our pay and notice if the desk closes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI could handle my calls, routing and checks in 2028, probably better than I do. The technicians might still visit homes until robots arrive around 2031, but Leon’s van wage alone cannot meet the mortgage and children’s costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tonight I’d ask Leon to lay out the mortgage, fuel and food bills with me, then stop the summer holiday deposit. Before 2028 I’d ask the company for written notice terms and ask my sister whether she could help with school pickups if I found paid technician-helper work; in the first year after AGI arrives, I’d apply only to posted helper jobs that cover our mortgage share.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m alarmed and I would be up late with the bills. Two years is not enough to turn a supervisor who books repairs into a qualified technician.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your sister?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask whether she could take the younger child from school twice a week for one term, not ask her to raise my children. I would make sure the schedule worked for her before applying for shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if helper work is not posted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep looking at the few service firms here and ask management about any paid transition period. I would not resign because a neighbour said somebody might be hiring.

say: I’d insist on a **human repair contact** after automated errors.
Management should state **pay and notice terms** for a closed desk.
think: Leon’s **van pay** cannot meet mortgage and children’s costs alone.
My **junior standing** gives me little shelter if the desk closes.
do: Review **mortgage and fuel** with Leon and stop the holiday deposit.
Ask my **sister about pickups** before seeking posted helper work at viable pay.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by the short deadline and bills.
S2.quote: I would not resign because a neighbour said somebody might be hiring.
fieldNote: She expects **2028 thinking AI** to replace her booking work.
Hands-on repair work may last until **2031 robots**, but she lacks those skills.
A helper move depends on **pay, vacancy and childcare**.

steps.text: Stop the summer holiday deposit after reviewing household bills with Leon
Ask her sister for two weekly school pickups only if the schedule works for her
Apply for posted paid technician-helper jobs after 2028 only if wages cover the mortgage share

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years lets the company train people before closing the booking desk, if it pays for the training. I’d still want a named person to fix a wrong repair booking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn enough about parts and home visits before 2031 to do a technician-helper job, though I do not like changing trades. Robots around 2034 may reach those visits too, so I would not count on a helper role forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I’d enroll in the company’s basic appliance-parts course only if it is paid and runs during school hours. I’d ask Leon to cover two after-school days while I shadow a technician on paid time, then apply for an advertised helper vacancy before 2031 only if the wage covers my share of the mortgage; after AGI arrives, I’d keep the role while paid home visits exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious rather than trapped. Five years would give me time to see a home repair before promising I can do one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Leon’s route changes on those two days?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I’d move the shadow days or ask my sister if she is available. I cannot leave my children outside school waiting while I learn a new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would passing the course be enough to make you leave?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would need a posted vacancy and a written wage, because we have less than a month saved.

say: I’d seek **paid parts training** before the desk closes.
A wrong booking still needs a **named person** to fix it.
think: A helper job might buy **time before 2034 robots**.
I need a **real wage** before changing work.
I need **childcare coverage** before I can practise on real visits.
do: Enroll in a **paid parts course** only during school hours.
Shadow a **technician on paid time** if Leon covers childcare, then seek a viable vacancy.
Keep the **helper role** after 2031 only while paid home visits exist.
feel: I feel **anxious** but have time to test the work.
S3.quote: I cannot leave my children outside school waiting while I learn a new job.
fieldNote: Her training depends on **paid daytime hours** and a childcare plan.
She wants a **written wage and vacancy** before leaving the desk.

steps.text: Enroll in paid appliance-parts training next spring only if it runs during school hours
Shadow a technician on paid time only if Leon covers two after-school days
Apply for an advertised helper vacancy before 2031 only if wages cover her mortgage share

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a decade gives the company time to keep current bookings accurate while training staff for site work. I’d ask for a written calendar of training dates and desk changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 by 2036, and our children would be grown or nearly grown, but the mortgage may still be there. I could build a cushion in ten years if Leon’s hours hold, yet I would not call the desk safe once thinking AI arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter Leon and I would set a standing 35 monthly emergency transfer only when his route pay reaches its usual level. I’d take a paid parts course after seeing it work for another colleague, then apply for a posted field service support role before 2036 if the wage keeps our mortgage paid; in the first year after AGI arrives, I’d stay there only while the company offers paid human visits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about having to start over at 53, but a decade gives me time to learn slowly. I would rather make one good career move than chase every tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut if that 35 cannot be saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would pause the transfer, not miss a mortgage payment. Leon’s route pay has to reach the usual amount before we move money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait for another colleague to take the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want to know what the job actually asks of someone who has done it. I have never used AI, and a good training advert is not proof that field work suits me.

say: I’d seek a **written change calendar** from management.
The company should keep **current bookings** accurate during training.
I’d ask for **paid course places** before the desk gets smaller.
think: The **mortgage may remain** when I am 53.
Ten years could build a **cushion** if Leon’s hours hold.
do: Transfer **35 monthly** only at Leon’s usual route pay.
Take a **paid parts course** after a colleague and seek mortgage-covering field support work.
Stay in **field support** after 2036 only while the company offers paid human visits.
feel: I feel **anxious** but able to learn slowly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. I would lose booking work before I can learn home repair, and Leon’s pay cannot carry the mortgage alone. Paid daytime training, written notice and a real helper vacancy with a wage on the page would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who collects a child when the parent is sent to a new shift. A training place is only useful if someone is at the school gate at three.

headlineQuote: A training place is only useful if someone is at the school gate at three.
portrait: **Bianca**, 43, is a new repair-booking supervisor with a bachelor’s degree.
Lower pay and **thin savings** leave her mortgage and two children exposed.
She has **never used AI** and trusts a tool only after real booking checks.
She considers **paid technician-helper training** only with childcare, a vacancy and a viable wage.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her booking job before she learns hands-on repair work.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid daytime training**, written notice and a posted helper job with a viable wage would help.
